title: Microwave vs fibre
text: Between Chicago and New Jersey, a few milliseconds decide who sees a price move first. Over that distance, the medium is the latency. This video puts numbers on that race, from a published study.

title: Why this route
text: Futures trade at CME's data centre in Aurora, Illinois. Stocks and options trade in data centres in New Jersey. Prices in one market move prices in the other, so the first firm to carry the news across can trade on it. That trip is a race, and it is run in milliseconds.

title: Glass is slow
text: Light in glass is slow. Corning gives its standard single mode fibre a group index of about 1.468, so light needs about 4.9 microseconds per kilometre. In air, the index is almost exactly 1, so a radio signal needs about 3.34. That is about a third less time for every kilometre. Over 1,000 kilometres, the difference is about one and a half milliseconds.

title: The distance
text: A 2014 study by Laughlin, Aguirre and Grundfest puts Aurora and Carteret, New Jersey, 1,179 kilometres apart in a straight line. At the speed of light, that is 3.93 milliseconds one way. Even a perfectly straight fibre would need about 5.8. Real cables follow roads and railways, so they are longer still.

title: The race, 2010 to 2012
text: The same study tracked the race. In April 2010, New Jersey prices reacted to Chicago within about 7.25 to 7.95 milliseconds. Spread Networks' new, straighter fibre cut that to about 6.65 in August 2010. By 2012, licensed microwave networks were estimated at 4.2 to 5.2 milliseconds. The authors put a well designed link at about 4.03, just 0.1 above the limit.

title: What microwave costs
text: Microwave pays for that speed. It needs line of sight, so over flat ground the study estimates a tower about every 70 kilometres: at least 20 hops. Channels are narrow, so there is little bandwidth. And Nasdaq's microwave FAQ names a heavy rain storm as the most common cause of outages, so its clients must also take the data over fibre.

title: What firms do
text: So firms send only what matters over the air: a compact view of the book, not every message. Nasdaq's FAQ says the number of price levels on its microwave feed varies, because bandwidth is limited. The full feed follows over fibre, a couple of milliseconds behind.

title: Takeaway
text: Over long distances, physics sets the floor. Air beats glass by about a third, as long as it is not raining. Next, back inside the server, where one socket option can cost you milliseconds.
